name: Eszopiclone
lead: Eszopiclone, sold as Lunesta and as generics, is a prescription nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic of the cyclopyrrolone class. It is the active (S)-enantiomer of zopiclone and is used for insomnia in adults.[1][11]

Its place in a looks-focused wiki is through sleep: people who sleep poorly often try prescription sleep aids to rest better, and rest supports skin, recovery from training and energy for the rest of a routine. Eszopiclone is one of the Z-drugs prescribers use for that purpose, and it has no approved appearance use of its own.

The FDA approved it in December 2004. It is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the US, and the FDA added a boxed warning in 2019 about serious injuries from complex sleep behaviors such as sleepwalking.[1] Wikipedia reports that the FDA lowered the recommended starting dose in 2014 after finding next-day impairment in some users.[11]
No published study has measured appearance outcomes with eszopiclone. The research base consists of sleep trials, reviews and safety studies.

paras: Eszopiclone is indicated for the treatment of insomnia in adults.[1][2] The American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline for chronic insomnia assessed individual drugs including eszopiclone.[3] Wikipedia says evidence supports use for up to six months, with some studies suggesting similar effectiveness at 12 months.[11]

subs.h: Use in appearance and recovery communities
paras: Members of fitness and looks-focused communities who discuss sleep tend to name sleep quality as a foundation for physique and skin, and prescription hypnotics sometimes come up in those threads as options a doctor may offer. Eszopiclone is not a recognised looksmaxxing compound, and none of the clinical research on it addresses appearance.

A 2003 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study tested nightly eszopiclone for six months in adults with chronic insomnia.[4] Other studies examined co-administration with fluoxetine in insomnia with major depression, and effects on respiratory arousal threshold in obstructive sleep apnoea.[5][6] A 2016 trial in Brazil compared eszopiclone with zopiclone, and a registered study examined it in nursing home patients.[12][10]

A network meta-analysis in The Lancet compared pharmacological treatments for acute and long-term insomnia.[7] Wikipedia notes a 2018 Cochrane review that found moderate improvement in sleep onset and maintenance, and a 2009 New England Journal of Medicine analysis of the largest phase 3 trial that described users falling asleep about 15 minutes faster and sleeping about 37 minutes longer than placebo; the same analysis commented on next-day functioning.[11] A 2015 American Geriatrics Society review advised avoiding this drug class in older adults.[11]

A matched cohort study associated hypnotic use with higher mortality, and reviews discuss safety in older adults; observational findings cannot establish cause.[8][9] No studies of appearance outcomes were found.

Labelled risks include CNS depression with next-day impairment, complex sleep behaviors (sleep-driving, sleepwalking), abnormal thinking or hallucinations, and worsening depression or suicidal ideation.[1][2] Common effects reported on Wikipedia include an unpleasant taste, headache, dry mouth, dizziness and daytime drowsiness.[11]
As a Schedule IV drug it carries risks of abuse, dependence and withdrawal.[1] Combining it with alcohol or other sedatives raises risk.[11]

Wikipedia lists common effects as an unpleasant taste, headache, dry mouth, nausea, dizziness, daytime drowsiness and impaired coordination, and neuropsychiatric effects including abnormal thinking, hallucinations, agitation, amnesia and suicidal thoughts. Sleepwalking and sleep driving are listed among complex sleep behaviors.[11]

The same article reports that use may lead to physical and psychological dependence, with risk rising with dose, duration, concurrent psychoactive substances and a history of substance use or psychiatric disorders, and that rapid dose reduction may cause withdrawal. It also notes that CNS depressants and alcohol add to sedation and that a 2009 meta-analysis found about 44 percent more mild infections than placebo.[11]

Its hypnotic effect is believed to arise from interaction with GABA-A receptor complexes near or coupled to benzodiazepine binding sites, enhancing inhibitory neurotransmission; the precise mechanism is described as unknown.[1][2] It is rapidly absorbed, peaks in about an hour, has a half-life of about six hours and is metabolised mainly by CYP3A4 and CYP2E1.[1][11]

Wikipedia describes eszopiclone as a positive allosteric modulator at the benzodiazepine site of GABA-A receptors. Absorption is rapid, with peak blood levels roughly 0.5 to 1.3 hours after an oral dose, metabolism runs mainly through CYP3A4 and CYP2E1, and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ketoconazole and clarithromycin, as well as grapefruit juice, are listed as interacting. A heavy high-fat meal is reported to slow its effect.[11]

Sepracor developed eszopiclone as the single-enantiomer successor to zopiclone, and the FDA approved it in 2004 under the brand Lunesta.[11] A 2007 European marketing deal with GlaxoSmithKline later fell through, and Sepracor withdrew its 2008 European application in 2009 after the agency would not treat the compound as a new active substance; it has been sold in several European countries under the brand Esogno since 2020.[11]
In the United States it is a Schedule IV controlled substance and prescription-only.[1][11]

In Europe, Sepracor signed a 2007 deal with GlaxoSmithKline and applied to the EMA in 2008, then withdrew the application in 2009 after the agency declined to treat the drug as a new active substance distinct from zopiclone; a version has been marketed in several European countries as Esogno since 2020.[11] Wikipedia also records that the 2015 American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria advise avoiding Z-drugs in older adults regardless of duration, and that a 2009 New England Journal of Medicine critique summarised the largest phase 3 trial as shortening time to sleep by about 15 minutes and lengthening sleep by about 37 minutes versus placebo.[11]

timeline.event: Sepracor withdraws its European marketing application.[11]
FDA lowers the recommended starting dose after next-day impairment findings.[11]
FDA adds a boxed warning for complex sleep behaviors.[1]
Sold in several European countries as Esogno.[11]

card.summary: A prescription Z-drug sleeping pill (Lunesta); sleep research only, nothing on appearance.
card.note: Boxed FDA warning for complex sleep behaviors; Schedule IV.

quick.overview:
Eszopiclone (Lunesta) is a prescription Z-drug for insomnia, the active half of zopiclone.

It has not been studied for appearance; the only link is the general role of sleep in recovery.
quick.mechanism: It enhances GABA-A receptor signalling near the benzodiazepine site, producing sedation.
quick.risks: The FDA boxed warning covers complex sleep behaviors such as sleepwalking and sleep-driving; other reported effects include next-day impairment, dependence and mood changes. It is Schedule IV.

angle.text: Eszopiclone is a prescription sleep medicine. People who use it for insomnia describe getting more sleep, which is the link to looks through skin condition, training recovery and energy.
